whatItDoes: Calculates your debt-to-income (DTI) ratio: your total monthly debt payments divided by your gross monthly income, expressed as a percentage. Shows where your ratio falls relative to common lender thresholds.
whyItExists: Lenders use DTI to judge whether a borrower can afford new payments, and households use it to check how much of their income is already committed to debt. A simple ratio makes both easy to see.
whoShouldUse: Borrowers applying for a mortgage or loan, renters checking affordability, and anyone tracking how much of their income goes to debt.
useCases: Check your current DTI before applying for a loan
See how a new car or home payment would affect the ratio
Estimate how much income is committed to debt each month
Track a goal of lowering the ratio over time
Compare your ratio against the 36% and 43% lender benchmarks
Decide whether to pay down debt before applying for a mortgage
instructions: Add up your total monthly debt payments
Read the DTI percentage and where it falls
Add a prospective new payment to model a future application
Re-run as you pay down debt or your income changes
examples: $1,900 debt, $5,500 income → DTI 34.5% — comfortably under the 36% benchmark
$2,600 debt, $6,000 income → DTI 43.3% — right at the mortgage ceiling
bestPractices: Include mortgage, rent, cards, auto, student, and personal loans
Use gross income, before taxes, as lenders do
Keep the ratio below 36% for comfortable headroom
Re-check after any change to income or debt
Factor in the new loan payment when planning an application
commonMistakes: Using net income instead of gross
Forgetting smaller recurring payments like card minimums
Ignoring that lenders add the new payment before deciding
Leaving out rent, which is a major monthly obligation
Checking DTI only once instead of tracking it over time
faq: Does this tool support multiple currencies? — Yes, select your currency from the dropdown. All calculations run locally in your browser.
Is this financial advice? — No, it is an informational metric.
What is a good DTI? — Below 36% is generally healthy; above 43% limits most mortgage options.
Front-end vs back-end? — Back-end (total debt) is what this calculator shows and what most lenders emphasize.
Is my data shared? — No, the ratio is computed locally in your browser.
What counts as debt for DTI? — Monthly obligations like mortgage/rent, cards, auto, student, personal loans, and other recurring payments.
Can I improve my DTI? — Yes — pay down balances, avoid new debt, or increase income before you apply.
